Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Electric Utilities Industry Faces Acute Debt Crisis

SARAJEVO, June 12 – Bosnia and Herzegovina’s electric utilities sector is facing a worsening financial crisis as mounting debt levels threaten the stability of major providers and raise concerns over the reliability of power supply, industry officials said Wednesday.

The crisis was triggered by a sudden tightening of credit conditions last month, when several leading lenders withdrew short-term financing from the sector. As a result, key utility firms such as Drina Power Group and EnergoBosna have struggled to refinance maturing debt, leading to payment delays to suppliers and contractors.

“Several of our member companies are now overdue on critical payments, which is putting the entire network under severe pressure,” said Mirza Kapić, president of the Federation of Utility Operators of Bosnia and Herzegovina. “We are warning that unless emergency measures are introduced, the situation could deteriorate further in the coming weeks.”

According to data provided by the association, the sector’s overall outstanding debt has risen to 1.2 billion convertible marks (BAM), up from 900 million BAM at the start of the year. Analysts say a combination of declining electricity demand and falling wholesale prices has undermined the financial position of utilities, many of which had expanded their borrowing to finance infrastructure upgrades in recent years.

“In the last quarter, we’ve seen a 12 percent drop in demand compared to the same period last year,” said Lejla Begović, an energy analyst at Sarajevo-based consultancy NovaEnergia. “That, combined with the credit freeze, has left utilities with fewer options to manage their obligations.”

Workers at several power plants operated by Drina Power Group staged brief protests on Tuesday over late wage payments, union representatives confirmed. “Our members have not received their full salaries for May and are worried about job security,” said Adnan Mehmedović, head of the Electric Utility Workers’ Union.

The government has convened emergency meetings with utility executives and financial regulators, but no concrete relief measures have been announced so far. “We are urgently seeking ways to stabilize the industry and ensure continued electricity supply to households and businesses,” said Energy Minister Nedžad Musić.

Industry officials are urging the government to provide temporary financial support or facilitate new lines of credit. “Without intervention, service interruptions and further layoffs cannot be ruled out,” Kapić said.

As the crisis deepens, sector leaders are calling for swift action to prevent a broader collapse within Bosnia and Herzegovina’s electric utilities industry. The situation remains fluid as talks continue.
